system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2171-12-30 19:46:00 to 2172-01-08 12:53:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex medical history including chronic lymphedema, morbid obesity, and recurrent cellulitis was admitted due to disseminated shingles and right leg cellulitis. She presented with a left-sided dermatomal rash and worsening leg swelling. Initial treatment included IV acyclovir and clindamycin. New lesions in non-adjacent dermatomes confirmed disseminated zoster, prompting a full 10-day IV antiviral course. Cellulitis improved after switching back to clindamycin from Keflex. A painful tongue lesion was evaluated by ENT and deemed a likely traumatic ulcer, not malignancy. Her chronic edema worsened with IV fluids, leading to blistering; wound care was initiated. Diuretics were restarted, and pain was managed with oral narcotics. Infectious workup showed no immunodeficiency. She was discharged home with services, on a stable medication regimen, with follow-up plans for INR monitoring, ENT evaluation, and skin care.
problems: Morbid (severe) obesity due to excess calories
Personal history of other venous thrombosis and embolism
Epilepsy, unspecified, not intractable, without status epilepticus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. My left leg has been getting more swollen and red again. I was just out of the hospital three days ago and it’s already back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you were on antibiotics recently. What were you taking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Clindamycin and doxycycline. I’ve been on doxy for years to prevent these flares. But this time, it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you have a PICC line already in place, which helps with access. We’ll start IV antibiotics again. We gave you clindamycin in the ER—any reaction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, that’s fine. But I’ve had bad reactions to vancomycin before—red man syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. If we need vancomycin, we’ll pre-treat with Benadryl and give it slowly to prevent that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been admitted so many times, I was hoping to avoid another one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll work to get this under control. Your labs show a slightly high white count, which supports infection. We’ll start with clindamycin and aztreonam for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it still cellulitis? It feels worse than last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the redness and swelling point to cellulitis. We did an ultrasound—no blood clot. And your heart and kidney function look stable, so this is likely related to your chronic lymphedema.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using a steroid cream on my legs. Could that be part of the problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That might be it. Steroids can thin the skin and make it easier for bacteria to get in. We’ll stop that and treat the infection more aggressively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’ve consulted Infectious Disease. They recommend switching to IV vancomycin because your infection isn’t fully responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I had red man syndrome before. Are you sure it’s safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you Benadryl first and infuse the vancomycin over three hours. That should prevent the reaction. It’s important we cover the right bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. How long will I need to be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess in a few days. If the redness improves, we can switch back to oral doxycycline and send you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg is looking a bit better today. The erythema has started to fade. We’ll keep you on vancomycin for five days total.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. My pain is also a little better with the morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing your pain. We’ve also restarted your diuretics—Bumex and Lasix—to help with the swelling from lymphedema.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been getting IV Lasix at home too. Should I keep doing that after discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice a week as before. We’ll coordinate with your home care team to continue that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray to check your PICC line. It’s in good position now after a small adjustment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many PICC lines. Should I consider a port instead?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good idea to discuss with your primary team. It might reduce complications over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—8.3 from 10.2. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m feeling less tired too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep going for two more days on vancomycin, then switch back to your usual doxycycline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I had a strange episode last night. I zoned out and my left arm was shaking for a minute or so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw the note. The nurse observed it too. You were post-ictal—confused afterward. Neurology was consulted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it a seizure? I take Keppra and topiramate every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology thinks it was an absence-type seizure. It can happen during illness, even on meds. They recommend continuing your current doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need a CT or MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Since you’ve had similar events before during hospitalizations and your exam is normal, it’s likely related to stress and illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’ll follow up with my neurologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ll schedule that for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is day five of vancomycin. Your leg is much improved—less red and swollen. We’ll stop the IV antibiotic and restart your oral doxycycline tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by the weekend. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled and your diuretics are set up for home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been forgetting to take my iron. Should I restart that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re adding ferrous gluconate. Take it four hours apart from your thyroid medicine and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ve switched you back to oral doxycycline. Your pain is managed with oxycodone and morphine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin? My INR was stable before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You stayed on 6 mg daily, and your INR remained therapeutic. Keep checking it at home as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my feet are itchy—could it be fungus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think so. We’re adding miconazole powder for athlete’s foot. Also, nystatin cream if you have thrush.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow. Your leg infection has improved, and your swelling is better with diuretics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Watch for redness, warmth, or fever. And no more steroid creams on your legs. They weaken the skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my seizure—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was likely triggered by this illness. Keep taking your meds and see your neurologist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another PICC soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your current one is stable. We’ll flush it daily. If you get frequent infections, ask about a port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll set up home health for your IV Lasix and wound checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll go home with services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I see you again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be discharging you today. Your primary team will follow up. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll keep my appointments and take my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve made great progress. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we added a lidocaine patch for any lingering nerve pain from past skin issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use it as needed—on for 12 hours, off for 12. And keep using clotrimazole if your mouth hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have the discharge papers ready soon. Your walker is here, and home health will visit tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad this flare is over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work to prevent the next one. Avoid skin trauma and keep your legs clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be more careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. And keep up with your INR checks and neurology follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll fax your discharge summary to your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. I see so many specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure they’re all updated. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. The transport team will take you out shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex medical history including morbid obesity, chronic lymphedema, obstructive sleep apnea, epilepsy, and recurrent cellulitis was admitted for worsening left lower extremity swelling and erythema. She had recently completed a course of antibiotics but symptoms recurred, prompting admission. IV clindamycin and aztreonam were started, then switched to IV vancomycin after consultation with Infectious Disease, given partial response and concern for resistant organisms. The infection improved over five days, and she was transitioned back to oral doxycycline. During the stay, she experienced a brief absence-type seizure with left upper extremity tremors, evaluated by Neurology, who recommended continuing her current antiepileptic regimen with outpatient follow-up. Her chronic pain was managed with oxycodone and morphine, and diuretics were optimized for lymphedema. She was discharged home with services, on her baseline medications including warfarin, with plans for home IV diuretic therapy, neurology follow-up, and avoidance of topical steroids on the legs.
